notes:
Some limits first. I didn't get to any of the modern-scholarship, Catholic, Orthodox or Lutheran sites, and I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for this psalm. The only "other view" material is how the Douay-Rheims and the old Greek and Latin translations (Septuagint and Vulgate) differ from the Hebrew, as reported by Bible Hub and the older commentators. For part 2, the sources do disagree on a few verses, but nearly all of them are Reformed, Puritan, Anglican or Baptist. I found no Methodist, Pentecostal or Lutheran teacher writing about these verses, so I haven't set out views by tradition.

## Background
- **When it was written.** The Pulpit Commentary leans toward Absalom's rebellion rather than the years when Saul hunted David. It splits the psalm into six parts: prayer (1–4), self-encouragement (5–8), what is troubling him (9–13), faith and prayer (14–18), praise (19–22), and a call to God's people (23–24). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Matthew Henry thinks it comes from the Saul years. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_031.cfm
- **Other Bible passages that quote it.** Guzik lists Psalm 71:1–3, Jonah 2:8 (echoing v. 6), Jeremiah's repeated "terror on every side" (v. 13), Paul in 1 Corinthians 16:13 (v. 24), and Jesus and Stephen (v. 5). Quoting Spurgeon, he notes that the heading "for the choirmaster" means a song full of grief was meant for public worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: "in your righteousness" means "because my cause is the righteous one." It also points out that v. 17 develops the prayer about shame. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Bible Hub's summary reads it differently: David asks that God's righteousness, not his own innocence, keep him from shame. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31.htm
- **Where readings differ (Luther).** Guzik tells how this verse puzzled Luther. Read alongside Romans 1:17, it brought him to see God's righteousness as something not condemning but the gracious justice given to sinners who trust in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/

**vv. 2–3**
- Clarke (in Guzik): "incline your ear" pictures leaning close to hear a sick or dying person.
- Maclaren and Boice (in Guzik): the prayer runs "You are my rock… so be my rock." Guzik adds that David asks "for your name's sake," not on his own merit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/
- Pulpit links the prayer for guidance to Absalom's revolt, where wise counsel mattered more than force. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- In the Douay-Rheims, v. 3 says God will "lead me, and nourish me." https://biblehub.com/drb/psalms/31.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit suggests the "net" may be Absalom's trick of asking leave to go to Hebron to pay a vow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html

**v. 5**
- **David's meaning.** Pulpit says David was not thinking of his soul leaving his body at death. He was handing over his whole self, body and soul, to be kept safe from his enemies. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31-5.htm
- Calvin: the act is ongoing. Whoever does this constitutes him the arbiter of life and death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-5.html
- Henry: David lets go of his request to be pulled out of the net and gives God his inner self instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-5.html
- **Jesus' use.** Jesus prayed these words on the cross (Luke 23:46), and Stephen echoed them (Acts 7:59). Ellicott and Perowne list Polycarp, Bernard, Hus, Luther, Melanchthon and others as dying with these words. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31-5.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/
- Lange (via Spurgeon, in Guzik): Jesus gave up his life with triumphant consciousness to the Father for resurrection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-31.cfm
- **Was the verse a prophecy of Jesus? (they disagree).** Barnes says Jesus' use doesn't prove the psalm was originally about him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-5.htm Coffman agrees: unlike Psalm 22, this psalm is not a prophecy of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-5.html Delitzsch disagrees in part: David's years of persecution are full of "types," patterns that point ahead to Christ's sufferings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-5.htm
- **What "redeemed" means (they disagree).**
  - Rescue from danger: Pulpit, Kidner (in Guzik) and Maclaren. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-5.htm
  - Possibly spiritual: Barnes sees no reason to doubt David meant rescue from sin, perhaps even by atonement. Gill allows both readings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-5.htm
  - Henry: Old Testament rescues were patterns of redemption by Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-5.html
- **Grammar.** Delitzsch: the past tense "you have redeemed" expresses faith that the rescue is as good as done. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-5.htm
- **Living it out.** Maclaren: committing yourself to God has to go with doing good (1 Peter 4:19). Self-will takes back what you entrusted. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/psalms-volume-1/into-thy-hands.cfm Spurgeon: these are words for living as well as dying. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/31-5.htm
- **Worship.** Bible Hub notes v. 5 in Jewish evening prayers. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31.htm Clarke (in Guzik) says the Latin "In manus tuas" was said by the dying, or by a priest on their behalf. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: "worthless idols" means idolatry, or perhaps witchcraft and fortune-telling. The LORD is their opposite, the "God of truth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Guzik: giving himself to God meant rejecting powerless idols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/
- The Douay-Rheims, following the Greek and Latin, reads Thou hast hated them that regard vanities, meaning God hates them rather than David. https://biblehub.com/drb/psalms/31.htm

**vv. 7–8**
- Pulpit: God "knowing" someone means looking on them with approval. The "open" or "wide place" means room and freedom to act. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Spurgeon (in Guzik): "Man, thou art known of God" is a greater comfort than "know thyself." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: "body" is literally "belly," which some take as the centre of physical life and the emotions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Poole (in Guzik): the whole person, inside and out, is worn down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/

**v. 10 ("my iniquity")**
- **Sin as the cause.**
  - Pulpit traces this to his great sin with Bathsheba. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
  - Henry: David pleads innocence toward Saul but admits he deserves what God has sent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-10.html
  - Gill blames his inborn and indwelling sin, unbelief, and perhaps a serious falling away. Barnes leans toward his corrupt nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-10.htm
  - Constable: his sins were partly to blame, but mainly evil men were. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-10.html
- **Suffering, not sin (a different reading).** Calvin translates "sorrow," because the Hebrew word can also mean punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-9.html Ellicott, citing Gesenius and Ewald, prefers "the suffering that follows on sin." The Septuagint and Vulgate read "poverty," as the Douay-Rheims does. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31-10.htm Cambridge notes that the Septuagint, Syriac and Symmachus read "affliction." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-10.htm
- Coffman, following Leupold, sees no reason to change the word, and says the verse rules out reading the psalm as a prophecy of Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-10.html
- VanGemeren (in Guzik): this need not mean physical illness. Mental anguish may have drained his strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-31/

**vv. 11–12**
- Pulpit: Absalom's long campaign of slander blackened David's name. Friends avoided him so as not to share his bad reputation. A "broken vessel" is worthless and only fit to throw away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Delitzsch: the vessel is one being thrown out and given up to destruction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-10.htm

**v. 13**
- Pulpit links the plotting to the council in 2 Samuel 17:1–14 ("I will smite the king only"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Delitzsch: "terror on every side" is word for word Jeremiah 20:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-10.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: through every trouble David has kept saying "you alone are my God." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Barnes: he said this while his friends were deserting him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-31.html

**v. 15 ("my times")**
- Ellicott: life's changes are under God's control, so enemies cannot win against one God means to save. The Septuagint and Vulgate read "my destinies." https://biblehub.com/psalms/31-15.htm
- Calvin: the plural "times" covers all the chances of life. Limiting it to his lifespan is "a cold exposition." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-15.html
- Henry: David doesn't dictate to God in his prayers; he agrees with God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-15.html
- **A predestination emphasis (Baptist, Calvinist).** Spurgeon speaks of divine arrangement and sacred predestination, and also of David's faith in handing his times over. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-15.html and https://www.monergism.com/my-times-are-thy-hand
- **A personal-trust emphasis.** A bible.org sermon grants that in one sense everyone's times are in God's hand. But David's times were there because David deliberately determined to put them there! https://bible.org/seriespage/new-years-1993-putting-my-times-god-s-hand-psalm-3114-15a

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: "make your face shine" comes from the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:25 and means "be gracious to your servant." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html

**vv. 17–18**
- Pulpit: "I have called on you" means "I have always been your true worshipper." His sins were lapses, not unfaithfulness. "Silent in Sheol" means their slander ends when they are removed to the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Delitzsch: v. 17 reads more as hope than as a request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-15.htm

**vv. 19–20**
- Pulpit: God has goodness stored up for the future as well as shown in the past. He hides his people in dazzling light, which no eye can see into, and keeps them in a "pavilion" (a cool arbour) away from slanderous tongues. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Delitzsch: the hiding place is the unapproachable light that comes from God's presence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-22.htm

**v. 21 ("a city under siege")**
- Henry: Keilah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-22.html
- Delitzsch: perhaps Ziklag, the turning point in David's fortunes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-22.htm
- Pulpit names Ziklag or Mahanaim but thinks it is probably a figure of speech. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Maclaren: best taken as God himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-one/psalm-thirty-one.cfm
- Coffman, citing DeHoff, suggests Ziklag. He says critics who date the psalm late, such as Addis, find the phrase meaningless. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-22.html

**v. 22**
- Barnes: "alarm" means terror that makes you run, not a rash opinion. God's mercy went beyond the psalmist's faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-22.htm
- Pulpit: God did not abandon him for this brief failure of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Henry calls it a hard thought of God that David admits to his shame. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/31-22.html
- A Biblical Illustrator sermon advises against voicing unbelief at all. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/31-22.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes take a gentler line: God values honest lament more than silent despair. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31-22.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Pulpit: "the faithful" literally means "those who stand firm." God strengthens those who do their best to take courage. "Hope in the LORD" means waiting for his help. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-31.html
- Delitzsch: the call to be strong echoes Psalm 27:14, and the waiting ends in "hallelujah." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/31-22.htm
- Bible Hub: v. 24 is used in many liturgies on the first Sunday of Advent. https://biblehub.com/psalms/31.htm
